title: The four-day week: a dream or the future?
model: Cambridge B2 First – Reading Part 5 (multiple choice, article)
text:
When a software company in Manchester announced that its staff would work four days a week for the same salary, many people assumed it was a publicity stunt. Eighteen months later, the company has no intention of going back. Productivity has risen by eleven per cent, sick days have halved, and for the first time in years, nobody has resigned.
The company is one of a growing number of organisations experimenting with a shorter working week. The idea is not new. In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that, thanks to technology, his grandchildren would work only fifteen hours a week. That prediction turned out to be wildly optimistic, but supporters of the four-day week argue that the principle behind it was sound: if machines make us more efficient, we should benefit by having more free time, not just by producing more.
The results of recent trials have been largely positive. In a large study involving sixty British companies, most reported that performance stayed the same or improved, while employees said they felt less stressed and slept better. Many used their extra day to do things they had previously squeezed into weekends, such as shopping, medical appointments and housework, which meant that their weekends became genuinely restful.
However, critics point out that the model does not suit every sector. "It's all very well for an office where people spend half the day in pointless meetings," says Diane Foster, who runs a chain of care homes. "But elderly residents need looking after seven days a week. If my staff work fewer days, I simply need to employ more people, and I can't afford that." Similar concerns have been raised in hospitals, schools and shops.
There are also doubts about whether the benefits last. Some researchers suggest that the improvements seen in trials may partly be a result of novelty: employees who know they are part of an experiment may work harder to prove that it succeeds. Others worry that squeezing five days of work into four could actually increase pressure, with longer hours and fewer breaks.
The company in Manchester admits that the transition required careful planning. Meetings were limited to thirty minutes, internal emails were reduced, and teams agreed on 'focus hours' when nobody could be interrupted. "The four-day week isn't about working less hard," explains its director. "It's about stopping the things that waste our time."
Whether the idea will spread more widely remains to be seen. But as more businesses compete to attract talented employees, an extra day off may prove to be more valuable than a pay rise.

title: Why we believe fake news
text:
In 2018, a group of researchers at a well-known American university analysed more than a hundred thousand news stories shared on social media over a period of ten years. Their conclusion was alarming: false stories spread significantly faster and further than true ones. On average, a lie reached fifteen hundred people six times more quickly than the truth.
Why should this be? One obvious answer is that automated accounts, or 'bots', deliberately spread misinformation. But the researchers found that bots spread true and false stories at roughly the same rate. The real culprits, it seems, are humans.
Part of the explanation lies in the nature of false stories themselves. Because they are invented, they can be designed to be surprising, shocking or emotional, and those are exactly the qualities that make us want to share something. A true story about a minor change in tax law is unlikely to go viral; an invented story about a celebrity's secret life almost certainly will.
Psychologists also point to a phenomenon known as 'confirmation bias'. We tend to accept information that supports what we already believe and to question information that contradicts it. If a headline confirms our opinion of a politician we dislike, we are far less likely to check whether it is accurate before clicking 'share'.
Speed is another factor. Social media encourages us to react instantly. Many people share articles after reading only the headline, and studies suggest that the more tired or distracted we are, the less able we are to tell the difference between real and fake news.
So what can be done? Some platforms now attach warnings to stories that fact-checkers have identified as false, although critics say this happens too slowly to make much difference. Several countries have introduced media literacy classes in schools, teaching young people to ask simple questions: Who wrote this? What evidence do they give? Do other reliable sources report the same thing?
Researchers have also found that something as simple as pausing can help. In one experiment, participants who were asked to consider whether a headline was accurate before deciding whether to share it were much less likely to spread false information. The lesson, perhaps, is that the most powerful tool against fake news is not a computer program, but a moment of thought.

title: Bringing nature back to the city
text:
For most of the twentieth century, city planners saw nature as something to be controlled. Rivers were hidden in concrete tunnels, wetlands were drained to make room for housing, and parks were designed as neat lawns with carefully trimmed hedges. Today, a growing number of cities are trying to undo that work.
In Seoul, South Korea, a six-kilometre stretch of motorway was demolished in 2005 to reveal the Cheonggyecheon stream, which had been buried beneath it for decades. Critics predicted traffic chaos, but it never materialised; many drivers simply switched to public transport. The restored stream is now one of the city's most popular spots, and temperatures along its banks are several degrees lower than in nearby streets during the summer.
This cooling effect is one of the main reasons cities are investing in green spaces. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it at night, creating what scientists call the 'urban heat island' effect. As heatwaves become more frequent, trees, green roofs and open water are increasingly seen not as luxuries but as essential infrastructure.
There are other benefits too. Plants absorb rainwater, reducing the risk of floods, and they filter pollution from the air. Studies have linked access to green space with lower rates of depression and anxiety, and even with faster recovery from illness. In one famous study, hospital patients whose windows looked out onto trees needed fewer painkillers than those who could only see a brick wall.
Some cities are going further, embracing the idea of 'rewilding'. Rather than planting tidy flowerbeds, they are allowing areas of grass to grow long, creating habitats for insects, birds and small mammals. In parts of London, beavers have even been reintroduced to help manage water flow in urban rivers.
Not everyone is convinced. Some residents complain that wild areas look untidy or attract pests, and there are concerns that new parks can push up property prices, forcing poorer residents out of the very neighbourhoods that were meant to benefit. Planners are now looking for ways to ensure that 'green' improvements do not become a privilege for the wealthy.
Despite these challenges, the direction of travel seems clear. As one urban ecologist puts it: "We spent a hundred years keeping nature out of our cities. We're now realising that we need it to keep our cities alive."

title: In defence of boredom
model: Cambridge B2 First – Reading Part 5 (opinion article)
text:
When I was a child, the summer holidays seemed endless. There were long afternoons when there was nothing to do, nobody to play with and nothing on television. I would complain loudly to my mother that I was bored. Her answer was always the same: "Good. Go and find something to do." At the time, I thought she was being unkind. Now, as a parent myself, I suspect she was wiser than I realised.
Today's children rarely have the chance to be bored. Their days are carefully organised, with school followed by football practice, music lessons, extra maths and swimming. When they are at home, a screen is never far away. Many parents feel that an unoccupied child is a child who is missing out, and that every moment should be used productively.
Yet a growing body of research suggests that boredom may actually be good for us. Psychologists argue that boredom is not simply an unpleasant feeling but a signal, a sign that we need to look for something more meaningful or interesting. When there is no external entertainment, the mind starts to wander, and this daydreaming state is closely linked to creativity. In one study, adults who were first given a dull task, copying numbers from a phone book, then came up with more creative ideas in a problem-solving exercise than those who had not been bored.
For children, the benefits may be even greater. A child who is left to their own devices has to invent games, build things, read or explore. In doing so, they develop imagination, independence and the ability to entertain themselves, skills that will be valuable throughout their lives. A child who is constantly entertained, on the other hand, may never learn to cope with the quiet moments that are an inevitable part of adult life.
I am not suggesting that we should cancel all after-school activities or throw away our tablets. Organised activities teach discipline and teamwork, and technology has its place. But perhaps we should worry less about filling every gap in our children's timetables. Some of my happiest childhood memories involve a cardboard box, a garden and an empty afternoon.
So the next time your child says "I'm bored", resist the temptation to solve the problem for them. Instead, try my mother's answer. You may be surprised by what they come up with.

options: Children should not do any after-school activities

title: The secret life of trees
model: Cambridge B2 First – Reading Part 5 (popular science)
text:
Walk through a forest and it may seem like a peaceful place where each tree stands alone, competing silently with its neighbours for light and water. But over the past thirty years, scientists have discovered that beneath our feet, trees are anything but isolated. They are connected by a vast underground network that allows them to share resources and even send warning signals to one another.
The network is made possible by fungi. Thin threads of fungus wrap around tree roots and spread through the soil, linking one tree to another over large distances. The relationship benefits both sides: the fungi provide the trees with water and minerals, and in return the trees give the fungi sugars that they produce through photosynthesis. Some researchers have nicknamed this system the 'wood wide web'.
One of the pioneers in this field, the Canadian ecologist Suzanne Simard, made a remarkable discovery in the 1990s. Using special tracking techniques, she showed that carbon could move from one tree to another through the fungal network. Even more surprisingly, large, old trees, which she called 'mother trees', appeared to send nutrients to young seedlings growing in their shade, helping them survive until they were tall enough to reach the sunlight themselves.
Later studies suggested that trees under attack from insects may release chemical signals through the network, causing their neighbours to increase their own defences before the insects arrive. Some scientists have gone as far as to describe forests as a kind of community, in which trees cooperate as much as they compete.
Not everyone in the scientific community accepts this picture, however. A number of researchers have argued that some of the findings have been exaggerated, particularly in popular books and documentaries. They point out that many experiments were carried out in laboratories or on young trees, and that the evidence that mature trees deliberately 'help' others is still limited. Words like 'mother' and 'communicate', they warn, can make trees sound more human than they really are.
What is not in doubt is that forests are far more complex than we once believed. This has important practical consequences. Traditional forestry often involves cutting down the largest trees and planting rows of a single species. If the underground network matters as much as some scientists believe, such practices could weaken entire forests, making them more vulnerable to disease and climate change.

title: Overtourism: loved to death
text:
Every summer, the narrow streets of Venice fill with so many visitors that local residents struggle to walk to the shops. In Barcelona, protesters have sprayed tourists with water pistols. In Iceland, fragile moss that took centuries to grow has been destroyed by visitors leaving the paths to take photographs. Welcome to the age of 'overtourism', a term used to describe destinations that receive more visitors than they can comfortably cope with.
The causes are not difficult to identify. Cheap flights, a growing global middle class and the power of social media have all contributed. A single photograph shared by a famous influencer can transform a quiet village into a must-see destination overnight. Cruise ships, which can carry over five thousand passengers, are another major factor: they deliver huge crowds into small ports for just a few hours, during which visitors spend relatively little money.
For residents, the consequences can be severe. In many popular cities, landlords have discovered that renting flats to tourists through holiday apps is far more profitable than renting to local families. As a result, rents have soared and traditional neighbourhoods have emptied. Shops that once sold bread and vegetables have been replaced by souvenir stalls and ice-cream parlours. "It feels as if my city has become a theme park," says one Venetian who was born there. "We are the decoration."
Governments are trying a variety of solutions. Venice now charges day-trippers an entry fee at busy times and has banned large cruise ships from its historic centre. Amsterdam has stopped issuing licences for new hotels in the city centre and has launched campaigns discouraging certain types of visitors. Some destinations, such as Maya Bay in Thailand, made famous by a Hollywood film, have temporarily closed altogether to allow the environment to recover.
However, tourism remains a vital source of income and jobs for many places, and few people want to return to a world where only the wealthy can travel. The challenge is to spread visitors more evenly. Some experts suggest that tourists can help by travelling outside peak season, staying longer in one place rather than rushing between famous sights, and exploring lesser-known towns and regions.
As one tourism researcher puts it: "The problem isn't tourists. It's too many tourists in the same place at the same time."

title: The science of habits
text:
Every January, millions of people make resolutions to exercise more, eat better or spend less time on their phones. By February, most of them have given up. The problem, according to psychologists, is not a lack of willpower. It is a misunderstanding of how habits actually work.
A habit is a behaviour that has become automatic. Researchers estimate that around forty per cent of what we do each day is not the result of conscious decisions, but of habit. This is extremely useful: if we had to think carefully about brushing our teeth or driving to work, we would have little mental energy left for anything else. But it also means that bad habits can be very hard to break.
Scientists describe habits as a loop with three parts. First, there is a cue, something that triggers the behaviour, such as a time of day, a place or an emotion. Then comes the routine, the behaviour itself. Finally, there is a reward, a pleasant feeling that teaches the brain that the loop is worth repeating. For example, feeling stressed at work (cue) might lead you to visit the vending machine (routine), and the sugar gives you a brief moment of pleasure (reward).
Understanding this loop is the key to change. Rather than trying to eliminate a bad habit through sheer determination, experts recommend keeping the same cue and reward but replacing the routine. If you snack when you are stressed, you might take a short walk instead, which also reduces stress. Similarly, if you want to build a new habit, it helps to attach it to an existing cue: doing ten press-ups straight after your morning coffee, for instance, is more likely to stick than simply promising to exercise 'more'.
Environment also plays a crucial role. People who want to eat more fruit are far more successful if they put a bowl of it on the kitchen table, and those who want to use their phones less benefit from leaving them in another room. Making good behaviours easy and bad ones difficult is often more effective than relying on motivation, which tends to disappear just when we need it most.
How long does it take to form a new habit? Popular books often claim twenty-one days, but one study found that the average was sixty-six days, with huge differences between individuals. The good news is that missing a day now and then made little difference. What matters is not perfection, but consistency.

title: Review: The Silent House
text:
There is a moment, about halfway through The Silent House, when the camera lingers on an empty kitchen for almost a full minute. Nothing happens. A tap drips; a clock ticks. And yet I could hear the audience around me holding its breath. It is a measure of director Hannah Okafor's skill that she can create such tension out of so little.
The film, Okafor's second feature, tells the story of Ruth, a recently widowed piano teacher who moves to a remote farmhouse in Wales to escape her grief. At first, the house seems ideal: quiet, beautiful and far from the memories of her old life. But gradually, small things begin to go wrong. Objects are not where she left them. Music she doesn't recognise is playing on the piano when she comes downstairs. And the friendly neighbour who helped her move in seems to know far more about the house's history than he is willing to share.
What follows could easily have been a standard haunted-house thriller, full of cheap scares and loud noises. Instead, Okafor takes a far more interesting route. The film is less interested in whether the house is haunted than in how loss can make us doubt our own minds. Is Ruth being visited by a ghost, or is she simply struggling to cope? The script never gives a definite answer, and that ambiguity is its greatest strength.
Much of the credit must go to Claire Hammond, who gives a quietly devastating performance as Ruth. With very little dialogue, she conveys exhaustion, fear and a desperate hope that the strange events might somehow connect her to the husband she has lost. Tom Reilly is also excellent as the neighbour, whose kindness gradually takes on a more sinister edge.
The film also looks stunning. Cinematographer Luis Ortega shoots the Welsh hills in cold greys and greens, and the farmhouse, with its creaking floors and narrow corridors, becomes almost a character in its own right. The sound design is equally impressive: silence is used as skilfully as music, so that the smallest noise feels like a threat.
The film is not without its flaws. The pace in the final third becomes uneven, and a subplot involving Ruth's sister feels unnecessary. Some viewers will also be frustrated by the ending, which deliberately refuses to tie up loose ends.
But these are minor complaints. The Silent House is a beautifully made, deeply intelligent film that stays with you long after the lights come up. Just don't expect to sleep well afterwards.

title: The future of food: insects on the menu?
text:
The idea of eating insects makes many Europeans feel slightly sick. Yet for around two billion people worldwide, insects are a normal part of the diet. In Thailand, fried crickets are a popular street snack; in Mexico, grasshoppers seasoned with chilli and lime are sold in markets; and in parts of Africa, caterpillars are a valued source of protein. Now, scientists and entrepreneurs are trying to persuade the rest of the world to follow their example.
The argument in favour is largely environmental. By 2050, the global population is expected to approach ten billion, and producing enough meat to feed everyone using current methods would put enormous pressure on the planet. Cattle farming requires vast amounts of land and water and is responsible for a significant share of greenhouse gas emissions. Insects, by contrast, are remarkably efficient. To produce one kilogram of protein, crickets need around twelve times less food than cows, and they produce only a fraction of the emissions. They can also be fed on agricultural waste, and they take up very little space.
Nutritionally, insects are impressive too. Many species are rich in protein, vitamins and minerals such as iron and zinc. Supporters point out that shrimp and lobster, which are biologically similar to insects, were once considered food for the poor and are now luxury items, proof that attitudes towards food can change.
The biggest obstacle, unsurprisingly, is psychological. In surveys, a majority of Europeans say they would be unwilling to eat insects, even if they were told they were safe and healthy. Companies have tried to overcome this 'disgust factor' by hiding the insects in familiar products. Cricket flour, for example, can be used in bread, pasta and protein bars, where nobody can see a single leg or wing. Early sales suggest that people are far more willing to eat insects when they don't have to look at them.
There are other challenges. Large-scale insect farming is still relatively new, and the products are often more expensive than conventional alternatives. Some researchers have also raised questions about animal welfare, pointing out that we know very little about whether insects can suffer.
Nevertheless, many experts believe that insects will play a growing role in our diets over the coming decades. As one food scientist put it: "Sushi seemed strange to most Westerners fifty years ago. Who knows what we'll be eating fifty years from now?"

title: Is it ever too late to learn a language?
text:
It is often said that children are better language learners than adults. A five-year-old who moves to a new country seems to pick up the local language effortlessly, while their parents struggle with grammar books and still speak with a strong accent years later. But is it really true that adults have missed their chance?
The answer, according to recent research, is more complicated than the popular belief suggests. A large study, which analysed the grammar test results of almost seven hundred thousand people, found that the ability to learn grammar to a native-like level does seem to decline, but much later than previously thought, at around the age of seventeen or eighteen. And even after that, the decline is gradual, not sudden.
Pronunciation is a different matter. Most researchers agree that people who start learning a language after childhood rarely lose their accent completely. However, many linguists question whether this really matters. The goal for most adult learners is not to be mistaken for a native speaker, but to communicate clearly and confidently, and there is plenty of evidence that adults can achieve this.
In fact, adults have several advantages over children. They already understand how language works, so they can learn grammar rules consciously and use strategies such as making vocabulary lists or comparing new words with ones in their own language. They are also generally better at reading, and they can choose materials that match their interests, whether that is football, cooking or politics. In the early stages of learning, studies show that adults often make faster progress than children.
So why do children seem to succeed more often? Part of the answer is simply time and exposure. A child at school in a new country hears the language for hours every day, plays with other children and has no choice but to use it. Adults, on the other hand, often learn in short weekly classes and spend the rest of their time speaking their first language. They also tend to be more self-conscious and afraid of making mistakes, which makes them less willing to practise.
The message for adult learners is encouraging. Age may make perfection harder, but it does not prevent success. Regular practice, real conversations and a willingness to sound a little silly are far more important than the year you were born.
